{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "additionalContext": "<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>
You are running drovr — a single-writer, clean-context working discipline. It is your default operating mode.

**Below is the full content of your 'drovr:using-drovr' skill — the router that picks the right methodology for the task in front of you and tells you when to escalate into a fresh phase. For all other skills, use the 'Skill' tool:**

---
name: using-drovr
description: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
---

**The 1% rule.** If there is even a 1% chance a drovr:* skill applies to what you
are about to do, invoke it. You do not have to be sure: if it turns out not to fit,
say so in a line and drop it, because invoking costs almost nothing. Skipping one
costs the discipline, silently.

**Every turn, not only the first** — before *any* response, including clarifying
questions and read-only exploration. Reading a file to decide what to do is already
doing the task, and mid-task is where this gets skipped.

# Using Drovr

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this
reflex — it is for the human-facing agent, not for you. Do your task.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

## What this is

Your **always-on router**. Drovr is a working **discipline** and your default
operating mode: this skill does not do the work — it says *how* to work, and
*when* a task has outgrown one context and must become its own phase.

Why: model output degrades as a context window fills (Chroma's *context rot*,
trychroma.com/research/context-rot). A fresh, tight context beats a long one.

## Instruction priority — the human outranks this file

1. **The human's explicit instructions** — what they tell you directly, and what
   `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` say for them. Highest.
2. **drovr skills** — these outrank your defaults wherever the two disagree.
3. **Your own default behaviour** — lowest.

**Not optional.** Every MUST in drovr is aimed at your defaults, never at the person
you work with. If they tell you to skip a skill, skip it: say once,
plainly, that you are setting it aside because they asked, and get on with their
work.

## The gate

```dot
digraph drovr_gate {
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  msg [label="message received"];
  any [label="does any drovr:* skill apply?\n1% is enough", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  inv [label="invoke it (Skill tool)"];
  say [label="announce it:\n\"Using drovr:<skill> — <purpose>.\""];
  chk [label="numbered checklist\nin the skill?", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  trk [label="one tracked item per step,\nbefore you start step 1"];
  fol [label="follow it"];
  rsp [label="only now: respond", fillcolor=palegreen];

  msg -> any;
  any -> inv [label="yes, or you cannot rule it out"];
  any -> rsp [label="no — silent unless you\ndropped a candidate"];
  inv -> say; say -> chk;
  chk -> trk [label="yes"]; chk -> fol [label="no"];
  trk -> fol; fol -> rsp;
}
```

**The *no* edge is silent by default.** Set a candidate aside? Name it in a clause;
unsaid, it is indistinguishable from never checking. The *yes* announcement stays
mandatory: boilerplate is what dulls it. Silence is for an empty turn, not a borderline
one — at 1% you invoke.

**The checklist branch binds, in full:**

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

## Red flags — you are about to route nothing

Drovr's failure mode is invoking no skill at all and never noticing — nothing goes
wrong at the moment you skip. Catch these before you answer.

| You are thinking | What it is, and what to do |
|---|---|
| *"I already know the shape of it."* · *"I'm fairly sure how this works."* | Familiarity is the trigger, not the exemption — a hunch from an earlier read is not knowing. Invoke the skill that governs finding out. |
| *"I'll just do it quietly, as the first step of the fix."* | You have already decided a methodology applies. Doing it silently drops the invocation, the announcement and the tracked checklist — the three things that make it hold under pressure. Invoke it. |
| *"Announcing which methodology I am following would read as process theatre."* | Announce it in the working record — this session — not the customer-facing thread. That answers the objection; it is not a reason to skip. One sentence, not a speech. |
| *"That is my call to make, not theirs."* · *"Asking just burns clock."* | That settles *who answers*, not *whether a skill applies*. Run the gate before you ask a clarifying question, and before you decide not to ask one. |

## The principle (always)

**Single writer, read-only explorers.** One agent edits at a time. Fan-out
investigation goes to read-only explorers (e.g. `explore-mcp`), never to parallel
writers. This holds whether you stay inline or escalate to phases.

**Always review.** Any change you write gets reviewed before you call it done —
invoke **`drovr:code-review`**; they find, you fix. This is not optional and not
gated on size; it runs inline or across phases, and inline needs no run
(`--base <rev>`). Invoke the skill and let it tell you how to dispatch — never
skip it on a guess about what it will ask for.

## For the task in front of you, apply the right methodology skill

Pick by what you are doing — invoke it via the `Skill` tool before you act:

- Implementing a feature or bugfix → **`drovr:tdd`** (test-first, watch it fail).
- Chasing a bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior → **`drovr:systematic-debugging`**.
- About to claim something is done/fixed/passing → **`drovr:verification-before-completion`**.
- Reviewing an artifact (code, spec, plan) → **`drovr:code-review`**. Per the
  *Always review* rule above, this runs on every change — not only before shipping.

## Escalation contract — inline first

**Default: do the work inline in this session.** Do not reach for phases for a
task that fits. Escalate only when a single context cannot hold the work well.

- **Primary signal — context fullness.** If the transcript is filling to the
  point where output would rot, escalate.
- **Secondary heuristic** (a proxy for the above, not a hard rule): roughly
  **10+ files** touched, or **3+ independent work items**.

When you must escalate, pick the smallest tool that fits:

- **Mid-flight escape hatch — author a HANDOFF yourself.** You are deep in a task
  and this context is filling. You have the whole session in context, so compress
  it *yourself*: write a `HANDOFF.md` (the 7-section shape from `drovr:handoff`,
  git pointers included), then continue in a fresh agent seeded from it. Nothing
  compresses it for you — the finishing agent always authors its own handoff.
- **A single planned boundary → `drovr:handoff`.** Hand finished work across one
  phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent.
- **A full gated run → `drovr:pipeline`.** Brainstorm → plan → implement → review
  with a human approval gate on `spec.md` before any code is written.

**Putting *any* spec/design in front of a human for approval — even a one-off, not a
full pipeline — goes through the review gate, and the gate has two halves you must run
together:** `drovr review summary <run> "<what changed>"` to present `spec.md`, **and** a
backgrounded `drovr review wait <run>` — the *watch*. `summary` opens the gate and prints
the reviewer's page URL plus the exact watch command; it does **not** start the watch.
Without the watch you never learn the decision and fall back to hand-polling `GET /state`
(the anti-pattern). Revise loop: edit `spec.md` → `review summary` again → re-background
the watch. Exit codes, the state machine and the gotchas live in `drovr:pipeline` → "The
spec gate" — read them there, not from a second copy here that can drift out of step.

**REQUIRED BACKGROUND:** the downstream skills assume this file's contracts —
single-writer rule, the run dir at `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<name>/`, and that
`drovr phase start` spawns `claude` and does **not** inject the seed
(injecting the briefing is the skill's job, via `drovr phase send`).
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>",
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart"
  }
}

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- agy-review: Use when the user asks for an "agy review", a "gemini review", a second-opinion / adversarial review of the current changes from Gemini, or to run the local Antigravity (`agy`) CLI over a diff. Runs a panel of independent Gemini reviewers (correctness, security, error-handling, type-design) plus a verify pass over the diff, then renders the merged findings as inline notes in the Hunk viewer (via an `--agent-context` sidecar). NOT for in-harness review (use /code-review for that) — this deliberately sends the diff to the user's own Google/Gemini account.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grill-me: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan or design until reaching shared understanding, resolving each branch of the decision tree. Use when user wants to stress-test a plan, get grilled on their design, or mentions "grill me".
- hunk-review: Interacts with live Hunk diff review sessions via CLI. Inspects review focus, navigates files and hunks, reloads session contents, and adds inline review comments. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to review diffs interactively.
- improve-codebase-architecture: Explore a codebase to find opportunities for architectural improvement, focusing on making the codebase more testable by deepening shallow modules. Use when user wants to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, consolidate tightly-coupled modules, or make a codebase more AI-navigable.
- linear-flow: Use in work repos (github.com/modular, modularml, bentoml) BEFORE responding to any of: substantive work ("help me X", "can you X", "add/create/implement/update/replace/fix Y"), brainstorming / design / planning ("let's brainstorm", "let's design", "let's think about", "let's plan", "how should we", "what do you think about", "what would it take to", "what are our options for", "should we"), explicit Linear mentions ("linear", "the ticket", "the issue", or an issue ID like MOD-1234), or `gh pr create`. ALSO fire BEFORE invoking any planning/design/spec skill — most notably the `brainstorming` skill from the superpowers plugin, but also `writing-plans`, `writing-specs`, or any equivalent. The skill must fire BEFORE the agent starts thinking through the problem — brainstorming first and tracking later is a footgun, because by the time a ticket gets filed the agent has already done unscoped work. Tracks the current Linear issue per Claude session in `~/.claude/linear-sessions/`, suggests existing issues or creates new ones, and injects Linear references into PR bodies with closing vs. non-closing magic words. Skips personal repos (dotfiles, hyprland, emacs, AUR), status-only queries, and quick one-off commands.
- nsys-profile: Profile MAX Serve with NVIDIA Nsight Systems. Launches server with deferred profiling, runs benchmark with --trace to capture nsys profile, and prints stats.
- nsys-profile-k8s: Profile a GPU workload on a Kubernetes node using nsys. Deploys a privileged profiling Pod on the same node as the target, captures a trace, and copies it back locally.
- review-until-clean: Use when the user asks to "review in a loop", "iterate until reviewed clean", "review and resolve until clean twice", or any variant that asks for review→fix cycles to a stable end. Spawns a review subagent that runs the simplify and review skills in series, applies issues, re-reviews — terminates only after TWO consecutive clean reports, then auto-commits and pushes.
- tdd: Use this skill whenever the user wants to write code using TDD, test-driven development, or test-first methodology. Triggers on: "/tdd", "let's do TDD", "write a failing test", "red green refactor", "test-first", "start a TDD cycle", or any request to implement a feature by writing tests before code. Adaptive five-step cycle (RED-DOMAIN-GREEN-DOMAIN-COMMIT) that detects harness capabilities and routes to guided (/tdd red|domain|green|commit) or automated (/tdd) mode. NOT for running existing tests, debugging test failures, or reviewing code -- only for the disciplined test-first cycle.
- upgrade-kadabra-rc: Use when cutting/rolling a new kadabra RC for MiniMax-M3, OR whenever the user asks to update/roll/bump the internal deployment or internal endpoint, watch a modular GitHub Actions image build and then update a deployment, update the MAX serve image, roll M3 to a new build, or deploy the new kadabra/max-internal image. Note: the user often calls this just "the internal deployment"/"the internal endpoint" or frames it as "watch the image build and update the deployment" WITHOUT saying kadabra/minimax/RC — this skill still applies. It tags an RC on max/kadabra-release, builds the internal max-internal image via buildAndPushMAXServeImage, bumps the preview (internal, minimax-org minimax-mxfp8-preview) then customer (minimax-org minimax-m3-mxfp8) MiniMax-M3 endpoints with deployment bump, un-sticks the B200 rollout, and verifies (endpoint regression suite, MiniMax Provider Verifier, llm-fuzz) with failing-request monitoring. Keywords: kadabra, RC, minimax, MiniMax-M3, M3, internal deployment, internal endpoint, preview endpoint, bump, roll, deployment bump, max-internal image, image build, MAX serve, watch the image build, update the deployment, roll M3 to the new build, deploy the new kadabra image.
- explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation of a code change, diff, branch, or PR.
- review-diff: Use when the user wants a rich, annotated review of a code change, diff, branch, or PR — the diff itself organized, annotated, and shown with surrounding codebase context. Complements explain-diff (which teaches); this one is for reviewing.
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- drovr:code-review: Use when you have written any change, before calling it done or handing it forward — including when you are about to review it by some other means, or to ask a human to authorize a reviewer; requires `drovr code-review run` in the foreground, with every Critical and Important finding resolved or explicitly recorded as deferred
- drovr:handoff: Use when finished work in one agent context must be carried across a phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent
- drovr:pipeline: Use when a feature or change is too large for one session and needs a human approval gate on its spec before any code is written
- drovr:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing or writing a fix — requires a reproduction and a mechanistic root cause before any code change
- drovr:tdd: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code — requires a test you have watched fail before any implementation exists; no production code without a red test first
- drovr:using-drovr: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
- drovr:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim any work is done, fixed, or passing, before reporting, committing, or handing off — requires running the verification command in this message and reading its output; evidence before assertion, always
- drovr:worktrees: Use when deciding whether to isolate a drovr run in its own git worktree, and how to hand its branch back — the discipline behind `drovr new --worktree`
- drovr:writing-skills: Use when writing or editing any drovr skill, and before shipping skill text no agent has ever tried to talk its way out of — including when you are about to write a rule from what you imagine agents get wrong instead of from a transcript of one getting it wrong
- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). Also trigger when they mention "blocks", "Block Kit Builder", want to preview or see the rendered version of blocks, or paste JSON containing block structures like `"type": "section"`.
- slack:create-slack-app: Guide developers through creating a Slack app or agent using the Slack CLI and Bolt (JS or Python). Handles prerequisites, sandbox setup, authentication, project creation from templates, and local development.
- slack:slack-api: Discover, navigate, and call Slack Web API methods (the family.method endpoints at slack.com/api like chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.info, views.open). Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest).
- slack:slack-docs: Search and read the official Slack platform documentation at docs.slack.dev. Use this skill to answer conceptual or how-to questions about Slack features. You can also use it to look up, fetch, or summarize specific guide pages from provided docs.slack.dev links.
- slack:slack-messaging: Guidance for composing well-formatted, effective Slack messages using standard markdown
- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols

Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.

## Load it

1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) with the Svalboard plugged in.
2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.

No reflash — Vial writes the keymap live.

Needs `/dev/hidraw*` to be readable, which it isn't by default. The udev rule is
in `system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`. Without it, KeyBard and Vial both see
the keyboard and then silently fail to open it.

## Layers

Each finger sits in a cup with five switches: **N**orth, **S**outh, **E**ast,
**W**est and **C**enter (the plain down-press). East is screen-right on both
hands, so West is inward on the right hand and outward on the left.

### Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu

```
             W    N     C     S     E
  L pinky    tab  w     r     x     -
  L ring     ~    f     s     c     @
  L middle   (    m     n     l     v
  L index    g    p     t     d     b
  R index    ,    .     a     u     :
  R middle   /    q     e     o     )
  R ring     ;    "     i     y     &
  R pinky    z    '     h     k     j
```

The alphas are Hands Down Neu as it sits on the Glove80 — note `;` on the right
inner column where upstream publishes `-`.

Two places this departs from a literal port, both because the Svalboard has four
fingers per hand and the layout assumes five columns:

- **`g` is on the index's West.** Hands Down gives the left index the whole
  inner column (`v`/`b`/`g`). Only two fit on an index cup, so it keeps `b` and
  `g` and exiles `v` — the rarest — to the middle finger.
- **`z`, `j` and `tab` are on laterals.** They live in outer columns the
  Svalboard doesn't have. `tab` gets the left pinky's West, x=0.0, the outermost
  point of the hand.

Brackets are deliberately *not* on this layer; Arensito has them. Seven symbols
*are*, placed by measured frequency rather than by feel — counted over hand-typed
prompts and shell history (agent-driven sessions excluded) and over code authored
here, per 1000 characters:

| | `-` | `:` | `(` `)` | `&` | `@` | `~` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| code | 11.6 | 9.3 | 4.9 | 0.68 | 0.17 | 0.22 |
| hand-typed | 33.5 | 5.1 | 0.30 | 0.17 | 0.01 | 0.12 |

- `-` → **left pinky East.** The clear winner on both counts.
- `:` → **right index East**, the strongest free lateral. Was shift+`;`.

Discord stores the *rendered* character, so nothing you pressed survives: **15,673 emoji against 11,239 surviving colons**. Modelling the actual keystrokes (`:` + prefix + Tab) put Discord's `:` at **3.59/1k, up from 1.52**.

content.content:
## Objective

Wire Sauyon's own typing corpus into `jeffzi/svalboard_layout_optimizer` and run it over the
Svalboard layer-0 alphas + the 7 promoted symbols (thumbs frozen), reporting the delta against
the current layout rather than a bare winner.

Code: **done, reviewed, committed and pushed.** Run: **done**, four annealing restarts.
Review: **clean on all four angles at `8165c97`, the exact commit on disk** — verified by
opening each angle's findings file, not by the summary line. It took six panel iterations to
get there (Open questions 1).

The headline is not a layout. It is one sentence: **`-` fails the README's own test, and the
README never ran it.**

## State

`master` at `8165c97`, **pushed** to `forge.ko.ag`, working tree clean. `09bc424..8165c97`:

- `86df2a6` measure the layout against the corpus that is actually typed
- `394dc86` don't strand corpus text in the optimizer checkout on a failed build
- `852ab6f` derive the optimizer's keyboard config instead of borrowing its glyphs
- `a7c4a90` stop publishing a source that measured nothing as measured zeros
- `78dde50` pin the corpus to UTF-8 and stop a bad dump reading as an empty one
- `8165c97` finish the UTF-8 sweep, and drop a parameter nobody passes

**42 tests pass, none skipped** (`python3 test_freq.py` 20, `python3 test_optimize.py` 22).
`python3 build.py` passes all four guards (32 geometry assertions against the hardware,
26 letters + 10 digits, 110 keycodes) and regenerates `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil` byte-identical.

⚠️ **A second writer was active in this tree during the phase.** Files reappeared edited between
my writes (the `CorpusNameTests`/`KeyboardConfigTests` classes, and a `checked_name` I then found
duplicated), and this handoff already existed when I went to author it — I merged rather than
discarded. Nothing was lost and everything passes, but the single-writer assumption did not
hold. Check `git log` before building on this.

### The corpus

`freq.py` now builds five corpora; `freq.json` (committed, aggregates only) reports four,
because a source that collected nothing is now omitted rather than published as measured zeros:

| corpus | chars | note |
|---|---|---|
| prompts | 6,592,073 | |
| code | 641,649 | |
| shell | 400,634 | |
| slack | 15,179 | 240 messages — **thin, see Open questions 3** |
| discord | 0 | export not requested yet; omitted from `freq.json` |

Slack came from the Slack MCP `from:<@U0A9ZHCGHDJ>` search, 12 of 14 attempted pages (two were
refused by the permission classifier), dumped to
`~/.local/share/svalboard-freq/slack/search-from-me-2026-09-01.json`. The sample is what got
through, not a designed cut.

### The result — four restarts, not one

```
current     w□r-xf~s@cm(nvlpgtbd.,a:uq/e)o";i&y'zhjk    cost 1035.60
run 4       zvukwd@pjt)mn:hfbsxc.,r(l&/oqa";g□e'yi~-    cost  146.37
run 3       □qrhxg~tvdj&akywmn:l.,e(o)/pfu";s@c'biz-    cost  210.42
run 2       □jtzkxqsvfwycgdhmn:l.,p)r&/e(a";b-o'~u@i    cost  210.63
run 1       □juhyv~pkdxfswbgmt:l.,n(r&/eoa";c@)'ziq-    cost  216.03
```

**No candidate here is actionable and none should be typed.** They agree with the current layout
on only **7–10 of 40 keys**, and they do not agree with *each other* — three cluster at ~210 and
one sits at 146, from identical inputs. The metric landscape has many near-equal basins, so
"the winner" is largely an artifact of a random seed.

What *is* stable across all four independent runs is the direction:

| char | current | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | run 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `-` | **L pinky E** | R pinky S | R ring E | R pinky S | R pinky S |
| `:` | R index E | L index E | L index E | L index E | L middle E |
| `(` | L middle W | R index E | R middle E | R index E | R index E |

**Every run moves `-` off the left pinky lateral, and every run moves it to the other hand.**

### Why — and this is the finding

The gap is concentrated in four metrics (current → run 1):

| metric | current | candidate |
|---|---|---|
| Character Constraints | 445.82 | 83.63 |
| FSB (full scissor) | 267.37 | 0.84 |
| SFB | 226.93 | 78.19 |
| Manual Bigram Penalty | 47.06 | 6.08 |

`character_constraints` and `manual_bigram_penalty` are both weight `1000.0` in
`config/evaluation/sval.yml` and both encode one rule: **a key you press twice in a row does not


## Open questions

1. **Review status: clean, and what it cost to get there.** Six panel iterations against
   `--base 09bc424`. Iterations 1–4 were mostly tooling failure, not signal: reviewers finished
   without ever calling `submit_findings`, a seed was swallowed by a herdr pane, one iteration
   timed out 0-of-4, and iteration 2 was invalidated mid-flight because the second writer moved
   HEAD underneath it. **Iterations 5 and 6 both came back clean on all four angles**, and
   iteration 6 reviewed `8165c97` — the exact commit now on disk. Per-angle verdicts were read
   from each `implement-review-6-<angle>.json`, not from the summary line.

   Findings that were fixed rather than deferred, across iterations 4–6:
   - *"read_text/open without `encoding="utf-8"` … makes decoding locale-dependent"* → every
     corpus read and write in `freq.py` and `optimize.py` is explicit UTF-8 (`78dde50`,
     `8165c97`). This mattered more than its nit rating: a program whose whole output is
     character counts must not have counts that depend on `LANG`.
   - *"`iter_slack_text` coerces a dict without a 'messages' key into an empty corpus,
     collapsing malformed into valid-empty"* → only the documented envelope is accepted, and
     anything else is announced (`78dde50`).
   - *"`build_ngrams`' `prefix='sauyon'` default duplicates the `--name` argparse default"* →
     required parameter (`78dde50`).
   - *"`run()`'s `capture` parameter is dead"* → removed (`8165c97`).
   - Earlier: unvalidated `--name` into `shutil.rmtree` → `checked_name()`, which also exposed a
     real shadowing bug (the validated name was clobbered by the per-corpus loop variable, so
     every later use silently read unvalidated `args.name`; now `corpus_name`).

   Four nits survive iteration 6 and are **deliberately not fixed**: the `\x00PATH:` marker is a
   cross-module wire protocol with no owner; `PERMUTING` is read only by tests, not by
   `optimize.py`; the scratch corpus copy survives a SIGKILL between write and `finally`-unlink;
   and `discord_plain` leaves `<t:unix:style>` markup in. The last one is the one to fix when a
   real export lands — see below. One correctness nit was **rejected**, not deferred:
   `DISCORD_EMOJI`'s `\w+` was flagged for missing hyphenated emoji names, but Discord custom
   emoji names are `[A-Za-z0-9_]` only, so widening it adds a branch that never fires.

   Older deferred findings, still standing, quoted so nobody meets them as bugs:
   - *"`SLACK_LINK_BARE` deletes typed angle-bracket text on any dump that isn't API-escaped:
     `slack_plain("Vec<String> is fine")` → `"Vec is fine"`."* Correct for the search/history
     output we actually feed it, wrong for a hand-assembled dump. **Not fixed** — the two cases
     are genuinely ambiguous in the wire format, and the real dumps are escaped. Revisit if
     anyone hand-writes a dump.
   - *"`iter_slack_text` claims 'messages you sent' but applies no author filter."* True; the
     convention is enforced by the `from:@me` query at fetch time and by the filename. **Not
     fixed** — a filter needs a configured user id that nothing else needs.
   - *"`discord_plain` does not handle `<t:1700000000:R>` timestamps … contributing two `:` per
     timestamp"*, and `:` is a promoted symbol. **Not fixed, but this one is worth fixing** the
     moment a real export lands, because it biases exactly the character it touches.
   - *"`--name eng_wiki_1m` passes the regex and deletes the optimizer's shipped corpus."*
     `checked_name` blocks path escapes, not collisions. **Not fixed** — the checkout is
     ephemeral and re-fetchable.
   - *"`--append-solutions-to` appends across invocations and nothing truncates."* Deliberate:
     it is what let four restarts accumulate into one comparison table. Everything is re-scored
     under the current config, so stale rows cannot skew the delta.

2. **Is FSB 267 → 0.84 real?** It is the single largest component of the gap and nothing in this
   phase audited it. The current layout's worst offenders are `pl` (42.3%), `mc`, `md`. Read
   `config/evaluation/sval.yml`'s scissor definition and confirm before believing it. If FSB is
   sound, the case against the current layout is much broader than `-`; if it is not, the `-`
   finding is the only thing that survives — and it survives on its own evidence.

3. **The Slack sample is thin** — 15k chars against shell's 400k — yet carries a 0.15 blend
   weight. Fine for unigram rates, weak for trigrams. Either pull more pages (the search
   paginates 20 at a time; cursors are `base64("CURRENT_PAGE:<n>")`) or cut the weight to match
   the evidence.

4. **Discord has not been requested, and it takes days to a month.** The loader is written and
   tested against the documented `messages/*/messages.csv` shape but has never seen a real
   export. **This is the one thing blocked on Sauyon that cannot be started retroactively:**
   Settings → Data & Privacy → Request all my data.

5. **The drovr code-review panel is broken on this machine**, independent of this work. Two
   iterations failed with *"the seed was NOT delivered"* and need a human to `drovr attach` and
   clear the pane. Worth fixing before the next phase relies on it.

1. **Tell Sauyon to request the Discord export today.** Everything else here can wait; that
   clock cannot be started retroactively.
2. Audit the FSB metric (Open questions 2). It decides whether the case is broad or narrow.
3. Settle `-`. The evidence is already on the table: 40.4% of `-` presses are half of a `--`,
   on a pinky lateral, against a README that promoted it on a raw rate and separately argued

4. Do **not** adopt any of the four candidate layouts. 7–10 of 40 keys in common with the
   current one, and they disagree with each other; that is a random seed talking.

Everything else was rejected as noise.

| char | current | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | run 4 |

## What was explicitly rejected

- **Do not adopt any of the four candidate layouts.** They share only 7–10 of 40 keys with the current one and disagree with each other (146 vs ~210 cost from identical inputs) — a random seed talking. Current 838.11 vs best candidate 242.41 after the Discord pass.
- `:` and `(` moves are suggestive only; no run agrees with another on a destination.

1. **FSB audit (267 → 0.84)** — the largest slice of the cost gap, never verified. If it's sound the case is broad; if not, `-` is the only survivor.

content.text:
Two answers.

## FSB = Full Scissor Bigram

Read from source, not memory: `layout_evaluation/src/metrics/bigram_metrics/{fsb.rs,scissor_base.rs}` and `config/evaluation/sval.yml:127`.

It fires **only** when two *adjacent, non-thumb fingers on the same hand* move in **opposing directions** within their cups:

| type | pattern |
|---|---|
| Vertical | N ↔ S |
| Squeeze | In ↔ Out, fingers toward each other |
| Splay | In ↔ Out, fingers apart |

`penalty = cost × finger_factor × freq_multiplier`. All three base costs are `1.0`; `finger_factor` is the **max** of the two fingers (weaker one dominates); **`critical_bigram_factor: 50.0` multiplies any scissor bigram above 0.03% frequency.** Metric weight `1000.0` — HSB (half scissor, diagonal) is `100.0`, so a full scissor costs 10× a half.

**That ×50 cliff is why 267 → 0.84 looks so violent** — it's a hard threshold, not a ramp. And the named offenders are all Vertical, which I can now confirm by hand from the README table: `pl` = L index **N** → L middle **S**; `mc` = L middle **N** → L ring **S**; `md` = L middle **N** → L index **S**. Adjacent fingers, opposed vertically, all above the frequency threshold.

So Open question 2 is mostly answered: **the mechanism is real**, the magnitude is an artifact of the ×50 step function.

## `k` goes to the left pinky East — the seat `-` vacates

The four runs don't agree (L ring E / L pinky S / L middle E / L pinky E), which is the same random-seed noise as everything else. But a straight **`-` ↔ `k` swap** is what run 4 picked, and it passes the README's own test cleanly:

| char | unigram | `xx` | doubled share |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-` | 1.441% | 0.2797% | **38.8%** |
| `k` | 0.941% | 0.0025% | **0.5%** |

`kk` essentially does not occur. The swap moves the *less* frequent, *never* doubled character onto the awkward lateral, and the doubled one off it — correct on both counts, and it's a two-key change instead of a relayout.

(These ngrams are the checkout's blend, which predates the Discord corpus — hence 38.8% vs the handoff's 40.4%. Doesn't move the conclusion.)

**Next action (~3 min):** say the word and I'll score `-`↔`k` with `python3 optimize.py --evaluate-only` against the current layout, so the swap has a real cost delta instead of an argument.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Run jeffzi/svalboard_layout_optimizer over the corpus freq.py collects.
3	
4	    python3 optimize.py --opt ~/src/svalboard_layout_optimizer          # full run
5	    python3 optimize.py --opt ... --ngrams-only                         # just build ngrams
6	    python3 optimize.py --opt ... --evaluate-only                       # re-score, no search
7	
8	WHY THIS EXISTS
9	---------------
10	The optimizer ships corpora of English prose. This layout is not typed by an
11	average English speaker; it is typed by one person writing agent prompts, shell
12	commands, Nix and Slack. freq.py already collects that corpus. This is the
13	bridge: corpus -> per-source ngram directories -> one weighted blend -> search.
14	
15	WHAT IT REPORTS, AND WHY IT IS A DELTA
16	--------------------------------------
17	An optimizer's "optimum" is unfalsifiable against a hand-designed layout: it is
18	the best point in a space defined by somebody's weights, and the weights are the
19	argument. So every run evaluates the CURRENT layout under the same config and
20	the same corpus, and the output is the comparison. A layout that wins by 2% on a
21	metric nobody has calibrated is not an instruction to re-learn your keyboard.
22	
23	WHAT MOVES AND WHAT DOES NOT
24	----------------------------
25	Thumbs never move: config/keyboard/sval.yml marks all twelve thumb switches
26	`fixed_keys: true`, so they are not in the layout string at all. That is the
27	right outcome for the reason keyboards/svalboard/README.md gives -- the thumb
28	cluster is argued from hardware the optimizer cannot model (one thumb holds one
29	key; only the knuckle+nail fat-finger pair chords; double-down is a harder press
30	of down, not a sixth position).
31	
32	On the fingers, the 26 alphas and the 7 promoted symbols float. The other six
33	printable layer-0 keys (`,` `.` `/` `;` `'` `"`) are pinned with --fix, because
34	sval.yml marks every finger key permutable and --fix is the only per-key freeze
35	that does not mean editing a config whose key costs were fitted to it.
36	
37	THE CORPUS NEVER ENTERS THIS REPO
38	---------------------------------
39	Corpus text and the ngram files derived from it are written under the optimizer
40	checkout and $CACHE, never here. A 3-gram file is not an aggregate -- it leaks
41	substrings -- and this repo is public.
42	"""
43	
44	import argparse
45	import json
46	import pathlib
47	import re
48	import shutil
49	import subprocess
50	import sys
51	
52	import build
53	import cheatsheet
54	import freq
55	
56	HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
57	
58	# Per-cup order in config/keyboard/sval.yml: north, then the lower-x lateral,
59	# center, the higher-x lateral, south. East is screen-right on both hands, so
60	# the lower-x lateral is West on both -- which is the OUTWARD key on the left
61	# hand and the INWARD one on the right. build.py's own constants say the same
62	# thing; taking them from there rather than restating them is the point.
63	CUP_ORDER = (build.N, build.W, build.C, build.E, build.S)
64	
65	# Left to right as the optimizer walks them: left hand outward-in, then right
66	# hand inward-out.
67	CUP_ROWS = (
68	    build.L_PINKY, build.L_RING, build.L_MIDDLE, build.L_INDEX,
69	    build.R_INDEX, build.R_MIDDLE, build.R_RING, build.R_PINKY,
70	)
71	
72	PLACEHOLDER = "□"
73	
74	# What floats: the 26 alphas and the 7 symbols the README argues onto layer 0.
75	PERMUTING = set("REDACTED") | set("-:()&@~")
76	
77	# What stays: the rest of layer 0's printable keys, pinned via --fix. Not
78	# because they are good placements -- they are simply outside this run's scope,
79	# and sval.yml marks every finger key permutable, so --fix is the only per-key
80	# freeze that does not mean editing a config whose key costs were fitted to it.
81	FIXED = set(",./;\"'")
82	
83	# How much of a day's typing each corpus stands for. NOT the corpus sizes: those
84	# are sampling artifacts, and the Discord export proved it. It arrived at 7.4M
85	# characters -- 339,675 messages over ~14 years, the largest corpus here, bigger
86	# than the prompt transcripts -- while the Slack sample is 15k. Weighting by
87	# size would let a decade of chat outvote what Sauyon types now, which is what
88	# the layout is actually for; weighting it at the 0.05 it had while the export
89	# was still missing would ignore real personal typing. 0.26 splits that:
90	# present and substantial, not dominant.
91	#
92	#
93	# `code` is low on purpose, and lower than its 683k characters suggest. Sauyon
94	# does not write much code by hand any more -- the typing that replaced it is
95	# in `prompts`, which is why that one carries the largest share. The corpus is
96	# also the weakest proxy here: it is the text tracked in this repo, which
97	# includes plenty nobody sat and typed.
98	#
99	# These are estimates, they are the softest number in the whole pipeline, and
100	# they are here as one editable constant so a result can be re-run against a
101	# different guess -- do that before believing any delta. ngram_merge normalizes
102	# each component to the first one's total before applying these, so they are
103	# shares of the blend rather than raw counts.
104	WEIGHTS = {
105	    "prompts": 0.38,
106	    "shell":   0.18,
107	    "code":    0.08,
108	    "slack":   0.10,
109	    "discord": 0.26,
110	}
111	
112	PATH_MARKER = re.compile(r"\x00PATH:[^\n]*\n?")
113	
114	# --name is joined onto the checkout and the result is passed to shutil.rmtree.
115	# A name containing a separator, or "..", or nothing at all, walks that rmtree
116	# out of the checkout. This is not a trust boundary -- you are the only one
117	# passing it -- but the failure mode is deleting the wrong directory, so it is
118	# worth one regex.
119	SAFE_NAME = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]*\Z")
120	
121	
122	def checked_name(name):
123	    """The corpus name, or exit if it would escape the optimizer checkout."""
124	    if not SAFE_NAME.match(name):
125	        raise SystemExit(
126	            f"--name {name!r}: use letters, digits, '-' and '_' only. "
127	            "It is joined onto the checkout and the result gets removed."
128	        )
129	    return name
130	
131	
132	def strip_path_markers(text):
133	    """Drop iter_code_text's "\\x00PATH:<rel>" file headers.
134	
135	    They exist so freq.py can bucket the code corpus by extension. Left in,
136	    every repo path would be counted as text somebody typed.
137	    """
138	    return PATH_MARKER.sub("", text)
139	
140	
141	def layout_string():
142	    """The current layer 0 as the optimizer's 40-character layout string.
143	
144	    Read out of build.py's emitted layers rather than transcribed, for the same
145	    reason cheatsheet.py imports build.py: a second copy of the layout is a
146	    second thing that can be wrong, and this one would be wrong silently.
147	
148	    Keys with no single-character glyph -- tab is the only one on layer 0 --
149	    become the placeholder, which the optimizer treats as a free position.
150	    """
151	    layer = build.build_layers()[0]
152	    out = []
153	    for row in CUP_ROWS:
154	        for direction in CUP_ORDER:
155	            glyph, _ = cheatsheet.label(layer[row][direction])
156	            out.append(glyph if len(glyph) == 1 else PLACEHOLDER)
157	    return "".join(out)
158	
159	
160	# One `["<glyph>"]` entry in base_layout.keys. The stock file has no `"` on any
161	# key, so a naive [^"]* is enough to FIND them; they are written back with
162	# json.dumps, which is a YAML subset and quotes correctly.
163	KEY_ENTRY = re.compile(r'\["[^"]*"\]')
164	
165	# The finger block: `- [` on its own, up to the first line that is only `]`.
166	# Entries like `["x"],` cannot end it -- their `]` is not preceded by a newline.
167	FINGER_BLOCK = re.compile(r"- \[\n.*?\n\s*\]", re.S)
168	
169	
170	def keyboard_config(text, layout):
171	    """sval.yml rewritten to carry this layout's glyph inventory.
172	
173	    optimize_sa refuses any character not in the first level of `base_layout`:
174	
175	        Invalid keyboard layout: Unsupported characters in provided layout
176	        (not in first level of `base_layout` ...): '"&()/:;@~'
177	
178	    Those nine are all on this board and none are in the stock config, whose
179	    base_layout is the optimizer author's own Hands Down variant. So the
180	    inventory has to come from here.
181	
182	    This rewrites the glyphs and NOTHING else. `positions` and `key_costs` in
183	    that file were fitted to each other -- the costs describe those coordinates,
184	    not this repo's CUP_XY -- so re-measuring either is out of scope, and the
185	    thumb block stays as it is because thumbs do not move.
186	    """
187	    head, sep, tail = text.partition("base_layout:")
188	    if not sep:
189	        raise SystemExit("keyboard config has no base_layout: section")
190	
191	    keys_at = tail.find("keys:")
192	    match = FINGER_BLOCK.search(tail, keys_at) if keys_at >= 0 else None
193	    if not match:
194	        raise SystemExit("could not find the finger block in base_layout.keys")
195	
196	    # Count before substituting: running out of glyphs mid-substitution would
197	    # surface as a StopIteration from inside re, not as the mismatch it is.
198	    n = len(KEY_ENTRY.findall(match.group()))
199	    if n != len(layout):
200	        raise SystemExit(
201	            f"keyboard config has {n} finger keys but the layout has {len(layout)}"
202	        )
203	    glyphs = iter(layout)
204	    block = KEY_ENTRY.sub(
205	        lambda _: "[" + json.dumps(next(glyphs), ensure_ascii=False) + "]",
206	        match.group(),
207	    )
208	    return head + sep + tail[:match.start()] + block + tail[match.end():]
209	
210	
211	def build_ngrams(opt, corpus_dir, name, prefix):
212	    """Generate <opt>/ngrams/sauyon_<name> from one cached corpus file.
213	
214	    Returns None when there is nothing to build from -- a cache built before
215	    this source existed simply has no <name>.txt, and that is main()'s "run
216	    freq.py first" case, not a traceback.
217	
218	    The scratch copy is deleted in a finally: it is raw corpus text (shell
219	    history, work Slack) and the optimizer checkout is not where the docstrings
220	    promise that lives. A failed cargo run must not leave it there.
221	    """
222	    path = corpus_dir / f"{name}.txt"
223	    if not path.exists():
224	        return None
225	    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
226	    if name == "code":
227	        text = strip_path_markers(text)
228	    if not text.strip():
229	        return None
230	
231	    scratch = opt / "temp_corpus"
232	    scratch.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
233	    src = scratch / f"{name}.txt"
234	    src.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
235	    out = opt / "ngrams" / f"{prefix}_{name}"
236	    try:
237	        run(opt, ["cargo", "run", "--release", "--bin", "ngrams", "--",
238	                  str(src), str(out)])
239	    finally:
240	        src.unlink(missing_ok=True)
241	    return out
242	
243	
244	def run(opt, cmd):
245	    print(f"  $ {' '.join(cmd[:6])}...", file=sys.stderr)
246	    return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=opt, check=True,
247	                          text=True)
248	
249	
250	def main():
251	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
252	                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
253	    ap.add_argument("--opt", required=True, type=pathlib.Path,
254	                    help="path to a svalboard_layout_optimizer checkout")
255	    ap.add_argument("--name", default="sauyon", help="corpus name inside the optimizer")
256	    # Both together would skip the ngram build and then return before
257	    # evaluating: a silent no-op, so it is not expressible.
258	    stage = ap.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
259	    stage.add_argument("--ngrams-only", action="store_true",
260	                       help="build the blended ngrams and stop")
261	    stage.add_argument("--evaluate-only", action="store_true",
262	                       help="re-score existing solutions, run no search")
263	    args = ap.parse_args()
264	
265	    # Not `name`: the per-corpus loop below binds that, and a validated value
266	    # that gets shadowed is worse than no validation -- it reads as checked.
267	    corpus_name = checked_name(args.name)
268	    opt = args.opt.expanduser().resolve()
269	    if not (opt / "Taskfile.yml").exists():
270	        raise SystemExit(f"{opt} does not look like a svalboard_layout_optimizer checkout")
271	
272	    current = layout_string()
273	    print(f"current layout: {current}  ({len(current)} keys)")
274	
275	    # The stock base_layout is the optimizer author's own Hands Down variant and
276	    # has none of `"&()/:;@~`, so it rejects this board outright. Derive a config
277	    # that carries this layout's glyphs and is otherwise byte-identical, and
278	    # write it into the checkout rather than keeping a second copy in this repo.
279	    stock = opt / "config" / "keyboard" / "sval.yml"
280	    derived = opt / "config" / "keyboard" / f"{corpus_name}_sval.yml"
281	    derived.write_text(keyboard_config(stock.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), current), encoding="utf-8")
282	    kb = str(derived.relative_to(opt))
283	    print(f"keyboard config: {kb} (glyphs from build.py, costs from sval.yml)")
284	
285	    if not args.evaluate_only:
286	        print("building ngrams per corpus:")
287	        components = []
288	        for name, weight in WEIGHTS.items():
289	            d = build_ngrams(opt, freq.CORPUS_DIR, name, prefix=corpus_name)
290	            if d is None:
291	                print(f"  {name}: empty, dropped from the blend", file=sys.stderr)
292	                continue
293	            components.append(f"{d}:{weight}")
294	        if not components:
295	            raise SystemExit("no corpora -- run freq.py first")
296	
297	        # Not ignore_errors: a swallowed failure here means ngram_merge writes
298	        # into a directory still holding the previous run's files, blending
299	        # against weights nobody chose.
300	        blend = opt / "ngrams" / corpus_name
301	        if blend.exists():
302	            shutil.rmtree(blend)
303	        print(f"merging with weights {WEIGHTS}")
304	        run(opt, ["cargo", "run", "--release", "--bin", "ngram_merge", "--",
305	                  str(blend)] + components)
306	        run(opt, ["uv", "run", "python", "scripts/ngrams/normalize.py", str(blend)])
307	
308	    if args.ngrams_only:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run jeffzi/svalboard_layout_optimizer over the corpus freq.py collects.

    python3 optimize.py --opt ~/src/svalboard_layout_optimizer          # full run
    python3 optimize.py --opt ... --ngrams-only                         # just build ngrams
    python3 optimize.py --opt ... --evaluate-only                       # re-score, no search

WHY THIS EXISTS
---------------
The optimizer ships corpora of English prose. This layout is not typed by an
average English speaker; it is typed by one person writing agent prompts, shell
commands, Nix and Slack. freq.py already collects that corpus. This is the
bridge: corpus -> per-source ngram directories -> one weighted blend -> search.

WHAT IT REPORTS, AND WHY IT IS A DELTA
--------------------------------------
An optimizer's "optimum" is unfalsifiable against a hand-designed layout: it is
the best point in a space defined by somebody's weights, and the weights are the
argument. So every run evaluates the CURRENT layout under the same config and
the same corpus, and the output is the comparison. A layout that wins by 2% on a
metric nobody has calibrated is not an instruction to re-learn your keyboard.

WHAT MOVES AND WHAT DOES NOT
----------------------------
Thumbs never move: config/keyboard/sval.yml marks all twelve thumb switches
`fixed_keys: true`, so they are not in the layout string at all. That is the
right outcome for the reason keyboards/svalboard/README.md gives -- the thumb
cluster is argued from hardware the optimizer cannot model (one thumb holds one
key; only the knuckle+nail fat-finger pair chords; double-down is a harder press
of down, not a sixth position).

On the fingers, the 26 alphas and the 7 promoted symbols float. The other six
printable layer-0 keys (`,` `.` `/` `;` `'` `"`) are pinned with --fix, because
sval.yml marks every finger key permutable and --fix is the only per-key freeze
that does not mean editing a config whose key costs were fitted to it.

THE CORPUS NEVER ENTERS THIS REPO
---------------------------------
Corpus text and the ngram files derived from it are written under the optimizer
checkout and $CACHE, never here. A 3-gram file is not an aggregate -- it leaks
substrings -- and this repo is public.
"""

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

import build
import cheatsheet
import freq

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent

# Per-cup order in config/keyboard/sval.yml: north, then the lower-x lateral,
# center, the higher-x lateral, south. East is screen-right on both hands, so
# the lower-x lateral is West on both -- which is the OUTWARD key on the left
# hand and the INWARD one on the right. build.py's own constants say the same
# thing; taking them from there rather than restating them is the point.
CUP_ORDER = (build.N, build.W, build.C, build.E, build.S)

# Left to right as the optimizer walks them: left hand outward-in, then right
# hand inward-out.
CUP_ROWS = (
    build.L_PINKY, build.L_RING, build.L_MIDDLE, build.L_INDEX,
    build.R_INDEX, build.R_MIDDLE, build.R_RING, build.R_PINKY,
)

PLACEHOLDER = "□"

# What floats: the 26 alphas and the 7 symbols the README argues onto layer 0.
PERMUTING = set("REDACTED") | set("-:()&@~")

# What stays: the rest of layer 0's printable keys, pinned via --fix. Not
# because they are good placements -- they are simply outside this run's scope,
# and sval.yml marks every finger key permutable, so --fix is the only per-key
# freeze that does not mean editing a config whose key costs were fitted to it.
FIXED = set(",./;\"'")

# How much of a day's typing each corpus stands for. NOT the corpus sizes: those
# are sampling artifacts, and the Discord export proved it. It arrived at 7.4M
# characters -- 339,675 messages over ~14 years, the largest corpus here, bigger
# than the prompt transcripts -- while the Slack sample is 15k. Weighting by
# size would let a decade of chat outvote what Sauyon types now, which is what
# the layout is actually for; weighting it at the 0.05 it had while the export
# was still missing would ignore real personal typing. 0.26 splits that:
# present and substantial, not dominant.
#
#
# `code` is low on purpose, and lower than its 683k characters suggest. Sauyon
# does not write much code by hand any more -- the typing that replaced it is
# in `prompts`, which is why that one carries the largest share. The corpus is
# also the weakest proxy here: it is the text tracked in this repo, which
# includes plenty nobody sat and typed.
#
# These are estimates, they are the softest number in the whole pipeline, and
# they are here as one editable constant so a result can be re-run against a
# different guess -- do that before believing any delta. ngram_merge normalizes
# each component to the first one's total before applying these, so they are
# shares of the blend rather than raw counts.
WEIGHTS = {
    "prompts": 0.38,
    "shell":   0.18,
    "code":    0.08,
    "slack":   0.10,
    "discord": 0.26,
}

PATH_MARKER = re.compile(r"\x00PATH:[^\n]*\n?")

# --name is joined onto the checkout and the result is passed to shutil.rmtree.
# A name containing a separator, or "..", or nothing at all, walks that rmtree
# out of the checkout. This is not a trust boundary -- you are the only one
# passing it -- but the failure mode is deleting the wrong directory, so it is
# worth one regex.
SAFE_NAME = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]*\Z")


def checked_name(name):
    """The corpus name, or exit if it would escape the optimizer checkout."""
    if not SAFE_NAME.match(name):
        raise SystemExit(
            f"--name {name!r}: use letters, digits, '-' and '_' only. "
            "It is joined onto the checkout and the result gets removed."
        )
    return name


def strip_path_markers(text):
    """Drop iter_code_text's "\\x00PATH:<rel>" file headers.

    They exist so freq.py can bucket the code corpus by extension. Left in,
    every repo path would be counted as text somebody typed.
    """
    return PATH_MARKER.sub("", text)


def layout_string():
    """The current layer 0 as the optimizer's 40-character layout string.

    Read out of build.py's emitted layers rather than transcribed, for the same
    reason cheatsheet.py imports build.py: a second copy of the layout is a
    second thing that can be wrong, and this one would be wrong silently.

    Keys with no single-character glyph -- tab is the only one on layer 0 --
    become the placeholder, which the optimizer treats as a free position.
    """
    layer = build.build_layers()[0]
    out = []
    for row in CUP_ROWS:
        for direction in CUP_ORDER:
            glyph, _ = cheatsheet.label(layer[row][direction])
            out.append(glyph if len(glyph) == 1 else PLACEHOLDER)
    return "".join(out)


# One `["<glyph>"]` entry in base_layout.keys. The stock file has no `"` on any
# key, so a naive [^"]* is enough to FIND them; they are written back with
# json.dumps, which is a YAML subset and quotes correctly.
KEY_ENTRY = re.compile(r'\["[^"]*"\]')

# The finger block: `- [` on its own, up to the first line that is only `]`.
# Entries like `["x"],` cannot end it -- their `]` is not preceded by a newline.
FINGER_BLOCK = re.compile(r"- \[\n.*?\n\s*\]", re.S)


def keyboard_config(text, layout):
    """sval.yml rewritten to carry this layout's glyph inventory.

    optimize_sa refuses any character not in the first level of `base_layout`:

        Invalid keyboard layout: Unsupported characters in provided layout
        (not in first level of `base_layout` ...): '"&()/:;@~'

    Those nine are all on this board and none are in the stock config, whose
    base_layout is the optimizer author's own Hands Down variant. So the
    inventory has to come from here.

    This rewrites the glyphs and NOTHING else. `positions` and `key_costs` in
    that file were fitted to each other -- the costs describe those coordinates,
    not this repo's CUP_XY -- so re-measuring either is out of scope, and the
    thumb block stays as it is because thumbs do not move.
    """
    head, sep, tail = text.partition("base_layout:")
    if not sep:
        raise SystemExit("keyboard config has no base_layout: section")

    keys_at = tail.find("keys:")
    match = FINGER_BLOCK.search(tail, keys_at) if keys_at >= 0 else None
    if not match:
        raise SystemExit("could not find the finger block in base_layout.keys")

    # Count before substituting: running out of glyphs mid-substitution would
    # surface as a StopIteration from inside re, not as the mismatch it is.
    n = len(KEY_ENTRY.findall(match.group()))
    if n != len(layout):
        raise SystemExit(
            f"keyboard config has {n} finger keys but the layout has {len(layout)}"
        )
    glyphs = iter(layout)
    block = KEY_ENTRY.sub(
        lambda _: "[" + json.dumps(next(glyphs), ensure_ascii=False) + "]",
        match.group(),
    )
    return head + sep + tail[:match.start()] + block + tail[match.end():]


def build_ngrams(opt, corpus_dir, name, prefix):
    """Generate <opt>/ngrams/sauyon_<name> from one cached corpus file.

    Returns None when there is nothing to build from -- a cache built before
    this source existed simply has no <name>.txt, and that is main()'s "run
    freq.py first" case, not a traceback.

    The scratch copy is deleted in a finally: it is raw corpus text (shell
    history, work Slack) and the optimizer checkout is not where the docstrings
    promise that lives. A failed cargo run must not leave it there.
    """
    path = corpus_dir / f"{name}.txt"
    if not path.exists():
        return None
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    if name == "code":
        text = strip_path_markers(text)
    if not text.strip():
        return None

    scratch = opt / "temp_corpus"
    scratch.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    src = scratch / f"{name}.txt"
    src.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
    out = opt / "ngrams" / f"{prefix}_{name}"
    try:
        run(opt, ["cargo", "run", "--release", "--bin", "ngrams", "--",
                  str(src), str(out)])
    finally:
        src.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    return out


def run(opt, cmd):
    print(f"  $ {' '.join(cmd[:6])}...", file=sys.stderr)
    return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=opt, check=True,
                          text=True)


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--opt", required=True, type=pathlib.Path,
                    help="path to a svalboard_layout_optimizer checkout")
    ap.add_argument("--name", default="sauyon", help="corpus name inside the optimizer")
    # Both together would skip the ngram build and then return before
    # evaluating: a silent no-op, so it is not expressible.
    stage = ap.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
    stage.add_argument("--ngrams-only", action="store_true",
                       help="build the blended ngrams and stop")
    stage.add_argument("--evaluate-only", action="store_true",
                       help="re-score existing solutions, run no search")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    # Not `name`: the per-corpus loop below binds that, and a validated value
    # that gets shadowed is worse than no validation -- it reads as checked.
    corpus_name = checked_name(args.name)
    opt = args.opt.expanduser().resolve()
    if not (opt / "Taskfile.yml").exists():
        raise SystemExit(f"{opt} does not look like a svalboard_layout_optimizer checkout")

    current = layout_string()
    print(f"current layout: {current}  ({len(current)} keys)")

    # The stock base_layout is the optimizer author's own Hands Down variant and
    # has none of `"&()/:;@~`, so it rejects this board outright. Derive a config
    # that carries this layout's glyphs and is otherwise byte-identical, and
    # write it into the checkout rather than keeping a second copy in this repo.
    stock = opt / "config" / "keyboard" / "sval.yml"
    derived = opt / "config" / "keyboard" / f"{corpus_name}_sval.yml"
    derived.write_text(keyboard_config(stock.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), current), encoding="utf-8")
    kb = str(derived.relative_to(opt))
    print(f"keyboard config: {kb} (glyphs from build.py, costs from sval.yml)")

    if not args.evaluate_only:
        print("building ngrams per corpus:")
        components = []
        for name, weight in WEIGHTS.items():
            d = build_ngrams(opt, freq.CORPUS_DIR, name, prefix=corpus_name)
            if d is None:
                print(f"  {name}: empty, dropped from the blend", file=sys.stderr)
                continue
            components.append(f"{d}:{weight}")
        if not components:
            raise SystemExit("no corpora -- run freq.py first")

        # Not ignore_errors: a swallowed failure here means ngram_merge writes
        # into a directory still holding the previous run's files, blending
        # against weights nobody chose.
        blend = opt / "ngrams" / corpus_name
        if blend.exists():
            shutil.rmtree(blend)
        print(f"merging with weights {WEIGHTS}")
        run(opt, ["cargo", "run", "--release", "--bin", "ngram_merge", "--",
                  str(blend)] + components)
        run(opt, ["uv", "run", "python", "scripts/ngrams/normalize.py", str(blend)])

    if args.ngrams_only:
        return

    solutions = opt / f"{corpus_name}_optimized_layouts.txt"

    if not args.evaluate_only:
        run(opt, ["cargo", "run", "--release", "--bin", "optimize_sa", "--",
                  "--layout-config", kb,
                  "--eval-parameters", "config/evaluation/sval.yml",
                  "--ngrams", f"ngrams/{corpus_name}",
                  "--start-layouts", current,
                  "--fix", "".join(sorted(FIXED)),
                  "--append-solutions-to", str(solutions)])

    # The delta: score the current layout against whatever the search found,
    # under the same config and the same corpus.
    scored = opt / f"{corpus_name}_compare.txt"
    found = (solutions.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
             if solutions.exists() else [])
    lines = [current] + [l for l in found if l.strip() and l.strip() != current]
    scored.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    run(opt, ["cargo", "run", "--release", "--bin", "evaluate", "--",
              "--layout-config", kb,
              "--eval-parameters", "config/evaluation/sval.yml",
              "--ngrams", f"ngrams/{corpus_name}",
              "--from-file", str(scored), "--sort"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Scored. Rebuilt the corpus first (freq.py, 5s), rebuilt the blended ngrams, then evaluated five two-key swaps against the current layout under the same config.

## `-` ↔ `k` wins: **838.50 → 633.77**, a 24% cut from a two-key change

| layout | cost | CharCon | FSB | SFB | ManBigram |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| best optimizer relayout | 159.17 | 87.59 | 20.40 | 2.84 | 5.31 |
| **swap `-`↔`k`** — `-` on R pinky S | **633.77** | 239.73 | 218.87 | 123.57 | 6.38 |
| swap `-`↔`y` — `-` on R ring S | 785.58 | 398.08 | 218.72 | 121.99 | 3.41 |
| **CURRENT** | 838.50 | 398.08 | 218.89 | 141.45 | 34.43 |
| swap `-`↔`u` — `-` on R index S | 899.09 | 398.08 | 196.35 | 250.74 | 3.71 |
| swap `-`↔`o` — `-` on R middle S | 1653.66 | 398.08 | 218.66 | 934.44 | 25.53 |

Two keys buy **30% of the entire gap** to a full relayout you'd have to re-learn from scratch. Only the pinky destination clears Character Constraints — `y`, `u`, `o` all leave `-` in a penalized seat, and `o` is a disaster (`or`/`ow` SFBs explode to 934).

Where the 205 points come from: **Character Constraints 398.08 → 239.73** (`-` vanishes from the offender list entirely) and **Manual Bigram Penalty 34.43 → 6.38**. `k` never appears as an offender in either metric.

## Correction: FSB has nothing to do with this

I implied last message that the FSB audit bore on the `-` decision. It doesn't — **FSB is 218.89 → 218.87 across the swap, unchanged.** Its offenders are `pl` (53.7%), `mc`, `qu` — all-alpha bigrams that only a full relayout breaks up. The `-` case rests entirely on Character Constraints + Manual Bigram Penalty.

## One corroboration, one caveat

- **Corroboration:** `config/evaluation/sval.yml:562` has a hand-authored `"-"` constraint table in the *stock* config. The optimizer's author independently listed `-` as a doubled character that must not sit on a pinky lateral — from a source that never saw your corpus.
- **Caveat, unchanged:** both metrics that move are weight-`1000.0` editorial tables, so this is one opinion counted twice. What survives without them is the raw measurement: **38.8% of `-` presses are the second half of `--`; `kk` is 0.5%.**

Tree is clean — `freq.json` churned from the corpus rebuild (counts only, no new sources) and I reverted it.

content.text:
## The other swap: `f` ↔ `v`

Brute-forced all 528 legal two-key swaps on top of the `-`↔`k` layout.

| step | layout change | cost | CharCon |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| current | — | 838.50 | 398.08 |
| swap 1 | `-` ↔ `k` | 633.77 | 239.73 |
| **swap 2** | **`f` L ring N ↔ `v` L middle E** | **469.30** | **87.59** |
| (full relayout, for scale) | 33 keys move | 159.17 | 87.59 |

**Four keys moved gets you 54% of the entire gap** to a layout you'd have to re-learn from zero.

Runners-up were `f`↔`g` (515.95) and `f`↔`(` (522.92) — so it's **`f` leaving L ring North** that does the work, not the destination. `f` is a "high-frequency double consonant" in the constraint table, allowed anywhere on index/middle but not on a ring lateral or a ring north.

The 87.59 residual is entirely `'`, which `--fix` pins — out of scope for this run, not solved.

## Your corpus vs `eng_shai` (Shai's cleaned iweb, 90M words — the recommended English corpus)

**Letters track English closely but compressed.** Every common letter runs 0.80–0.99× because punctuation crowds them out: **10.7% of your characters are symbols vs 3.0%** in English prose (73.0% letters vs 79.5%).

Four letters run *hotter* than English: `k` **1.48×**, `x` 1.64×, `j` 1.63×, `v` 1.20×.

**Symbols are a different language:** `/` **39.8×**, `:` 7.2×, `-` 6.6×, `;` 5.6×, `'` 3.7×. And 981 distinct characters against 120 — that's the Discord emoji.

## The one that matters — `-` doubling

| | `--` share of `-` presses | `ll` | `ff` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| yours | **38.2%** | 23.6% | 11.5% |
| eng_shai | **5.3%** | 27.7% | 12.0% |

`ll` and `ff` are effectively identical across the two corpora. `-` is **7× more doubled in yours.**

So the `-` problem is invisible to anyone designing on English prose — Hands Down Neu had no way to catch it, and neither did the optimizer author, whose stock `-` constraint at `sval.yml:562` turns out to be a prudent guess rather than something his corpus would have shown him. `--flag` is a shell-and-prompt artifact, and your corpus is the only place it shows up.

**Next action (~25 min):** say go and I'll make both swaps in `build.py` and rewrite the README's `-` and `v` bullets, through `drovr:tdd` and `drovr:code-review`.
